paras: The mob shooting of Len Beauchamps was an attack on a Black man on the night of October 30, 1903, in which a mob took him from officers and shot him on suspicion of assaulting a white girl; the fullest dispatch placed it at Sedalia, Missouri, while others gave the place as "Vidalia." Beauchamps survived the shooting but was reported so badly hurt that he was not expected to recover, and evidence was then said to point to another Black man, who escaped the mob. Newspapers that carried the story presented it as a case of a mob attacking "the wrong negro."

According to a dispatch dated Sedalia, Mo., October 31, a white girl had been assaulted on the outskirts of the city, and Beauchamps, described as "a negro," was in the custody of officers when the mob reached him. None of the reports names the girl or explains why Beauchamps was suspected.

On the night of Friday, October 30, the mob took Beauchamps from the officers and shot him "full of holes," on the theory that he was the assailant. Its members then dispersed, "satisfied that they had killed the right man," but Beauchamps was later found alive and protesting that he was innocent. What the Spokane Press called "better evidence" next pointed to another Black man as the girl's assailant, and the mob went after him. In the Spokane account he managed to elude his pursuers, while the Walla Walla and Lewiston versions said only that the mob was pursuing him.

Beauchamps's wounds were described as grave: the Spokane Press said he "can not recover," the Walla Walla Evening Statesman that he would "probably die," and the Lewiston Evening Teller, three days after the shooting, that he "may die." The Spokane Press added that the mob's leaders were afraid to make themselves known because of the legal trouble they would face if it were proved they had caused his death. No later report of Beauchamps's death or recovery, of arrests of mob members, or of the capture of the second suspect appears in the coverage.

The episode appears only in three white papers of the Pacific Northwest, each of which ran a short telegraphic item on its front page. The Spokane Press of October 31 gave it the fullest treatment, under the headline "Vengeance of Mob upon the Innocent" and a second headline, "Negro is Lynched and Shot. While the Guilty Man Escapes," although its own text said Beauchamps had not been killed. Its dispatch opened, "Another mob has done its terrible work and later finds that it attacked the wrong negro," and blamed "the fickle spirit of the roused mob" for the second chase.

The same day the Walla Walla Evening Statesman ran a shorter, unsigned version headed "Mobbed Wrong Man Is Proven Innogent," with a subhead calling the attackers "Lynchers," and stated that the man "has been proven innocent." On November 2 the Lewiston Evening Teller printed a nearly identical special telegram under "Mob Shot Wrong Man." Neither of these two papers named the victim, and neither added comment beyond its headline.

The reports disagree on the place: the Spokane Press dated its story from Sedalia, Mo., the Walla Walla paper from "Vidalia," and the Lewiston paper from "VIDALIA, Ind." Because the three items share their details and much of their wording, they appear to be versions of one wire report rather than separate events, and no Missouri or Indiana paper in the coverage confirms either location. They also differ on Beauchamps's innocence: the shorter versions treated it as established, while the Spokane Press reported only that he protested it and that suspicion had shifted to another man.

reader.title: Mob shooting of Len Beauchamps
bases: A mob took a Black man accused of assaulting a white girl from officers' custody and shot him, believing it had killed him, and the Spokane Press headlined it 'Negro is Lynched'; he was alive at last report, so this is an attempted lynching (A1, A2, A5).

The three papers that carried it ran close variants of one telegraphic dispatch (A1-A3, A4, A5), with no local Missouri report or Black-press account, so there is in effect one source, and it disagrees with itself on the place.

framing.detail: The Spokane Press headlined it 'Vengeance of Mob upon the Innocent', opened 'Another mob has done its terrible work', and spoke of 'the fickle spirit of the roused mob', while a second headline said 'Negro is Lynched and Shot'.

The Walla Walla Evening Statesman ran the wire item as 'Mobbed Wrong Man is Proven Innogent' with the subhead 'Lynchers Are Now Chasing Another Negro', stressing the victim's innocence without comment.
The Lewiston Evening Teller printed it as a special telegram under 'Mob Shot Wrong Man'.

conflicts.note: The three items share details and wording and look like one wire story with a garbled dateline; only the Spokane Press version names the victim and gives a fuller text, but no Missouri or Indiana paper in the coverage confirms either place.
